description.text:
The 53 promotional cards Wizards of the Coast numbered between July 1999 and March 2003, each with a black star reading PROMO where the expansion symbol would go, which gave Black Star Promos their name.

Most were monthly Pokémon League prizes, from the Pikachu of July 1999 to the Snorlax of August 2002. The films brought others: Electabuzz, Mewtwo, Pikachu and Dragonite at screenings of Pokémon: The First Movie from November 1999, with a gold stamp reading "Kids WB Presents: Pokémon: The First Movie" on the art; Articuno, Moltres and Zapdos for The Power of One, with art different from their Japanese promos; Entei for Spell of the Unown; and Celebi for Pokémon 4Ever, with more cards in the home video releases. Nintendo added its own, in Nintendo Power magazine, the Game Boy Trading Card Game and the Pokémon Stadium bundle, and the opening of Pokémon Center New York in November 2001 brought the Pokémon Center and Lucky Stadium cards.

Every card had come out in Japan first, as a promo or in a special set, except the two Mew (8 and 9), which came from the Japanese Fossil expansion. The set ended when Wizards lost its license.

description.text:
The first Pokémon League promo, given out from July 1999. Wizards of the Coast's Pokémon League started in June 1999, after prototype leagues that spring, and was run in toy, book and game shops across the United States. League members earned points for turning up, playing, trading and teaching the game, stamped into a badge book, and each season had a promo card: one copy at 250 points and a second at 500.

Keiji Kinebuchi's Pikachu among ivy leaves, known to collectors as Ivy Pikachu, was one of Japan's first two promo cards, given with the November 1996 issue of CoroCoro Comic in October 1996. A copy with a 1st Edition stamp also exists: some turned up in 1st Edition Jungle boosters, and Wizards gave others to some of the players it picked out in its 2001 Create a Baby Pokémon contest.

description.text:
This copy carries a stamp added by LPPCollecting, an Italian card shop and distributor that runs Pokémon tournaments and Pokémon Days in Italy. It is not an official Pokémon stamp. This one reads "LPPCollecting – Per 2 o piu' giogatori", a misspelling of the Italian for "for 2 or more players", and was given out at the Italian Pokémon Day at Mirabilandia on 18 and 19 June 2011. LPPCollecting's own listing counts 1,191 printed.

When the misspelling was noticed the stamp was corrected to "giocatori" (243 printed, by the same listing), and a version worded in English was made around the same time. Upside-down copies of both Italian stamps exist (57 and 6), and from December 2021 LPPCollecting gave a "20th Anniversario" stamped copy with larger orders from its webshop, for its twentieth anniversary.

description.text:
The 1st Edition-stamped Ivy Pikachu. In its weekly Pokémon card game chat of 23 March 2000, Wizards of the Coast said this promo had been inadvertently mixed in with a few Jungle boosters; 1st Edition Jungle packs had carried the line "Capture the rare Pikachu card! Look on inside wrapper!".

Its only known official release was as a prize in Wizards' first fan card contest, Create a Baby Pokémon, which began in January 2001. Wizards picked 16 entries as favorites and posted them on its site in March 2001; some of those entrants received several copies of this card, though not all of them got one.

Pokémon: The First Movie opened in North American cinemas in November 1999, and select theaters gave away four exclusive cards, Electabuzz, Pikachu, Mewtwo and Dragonite, handed out in random order over the weeks the film played there. Each has a gold "Kids WB Presents Pokémon The First Movie" stamp on its picture, and the packs held an insert advertising the new Pokémon League.

Ken Sugimori's Electabuzz first came in Japan with the 1997 Official Card File, a binder for the cards sold from June 1997. In 2002 it came back as the "classic" promo of the Fighting season in the Pokémon League's third year, Energize Your Game, whose seasons each gave an older promo first and a new one after it.

description.text:
This copy is the Pokémon The First Movie promo, gold "Kids WB Presents" stamp and all, printed in Japan on Japanese card stock. It came with the Japanese VHS of the "Kanzenban" (complete edition) of Mewtwo Strikes Back, the longer cut made for the American release, which went on sale in Japan in November 1999 to coincide with the film's US premiere and was sold as the American version. The shrink wrap advertised the card as a "US commemorative card", and Japanese collectors still call it the US Version.

It is very hard to tell from the cinema card: its colors are lighter and more washed out, its surface is smoother, and since Japanese stock has no black core, light shines through it far more. The folded plastic sleeve it came in is the surest sign of one.

It was later packed with the soundtrack of Pokémon: The First Movie, which Atlantic Records released on 9 November 1999. description.text:
This copy of the League Mew has a glossy finish. It came with Comic GOTTA, Shogakukan's monthly manga magazine for teenage boys, in 2000. The magazine also gave away a glossy French copy of Pikachu 4. Comic GOTTA had replaced Hyper CoroCoro, the older readers' offshoot of CoroCoro Comic, in December 1999, and it closed with its July 2001 issue.

Nothing but the gloss sets it apart, so it is very hard to tell from the ordinary Mew 8 in photographs.

League members earned points for turning up, playing, trading and teaching the game, stamped into a badge book, and each season had a promo card: one copy at 250 points and a second at 500.

In Japan the game, Pokémon Card GB, had come out on 18 December 1998, and Kagemaru Himeno's Meowth, with its single attack Cat Punch, came with the February 1999 issue of CoroCoro Comic as "GB Meowth". A non-holo copy printed in Japan came with the JR Pokémon Stamp Rally of 2000, and is described on its own variant.

description.text: The non-holo Meowth 10 is an English card issued only in Japan, for the JR Pokémon Stamp Rally of 2000. Unlike the rally's Eevee and Mewtwo, which were prizes for finishing a course, the Meowth, collectors say, came in a pack of goodies sold with a prepaid rail pass for the rally, on the JR West line, while the Eevee and Mewtwo were JR East prizes. Wizards of the Coast's own Meowth 10, the Game Boy promo, is holofoil, so this plain copy is easy to tell apart.

In Japan, a non-holo copy was a prize in the JR East Pokémon Stamp Rally of 2000.

Finishing the silver course won the Mewtwo 12 instead. Wizards of the Coast printed the Eevee 11 it gave out in the West in holofoil, so this plain-background copy is easy to tell apart.

description.text:
This copy is the English Mewtwo 12 printed in Japan on Japanese card stock, the prize for completing the silver course of the JR Pokémon Stamp Rally in August 2000. Children traveled Tokyo's Yamanote Line collecting a stamp at each station in a rally passport; finishing the gold course won the non-holo Eevee 11 instead.

The ordinary Mewtwo 12 is non-holo too, so this is the hardest of the rally cards to spot: side by side its purple is slightly lighter, and little else differs. It was handed out in a booklet, and a copy still in one is the surest way to know it.

In Japan the same card, which had first existed only inside the game, came taped inside the back cover of the official guidebook to Pokémon Card GB. Ken Sugimori's picture is the one he drew for the 1998 Trade Please campaign's Venusaur, framed wider.

Rumours that copies were already out, and that the promo had been held back because it was printed without HP, went round in May 2000, three months before the corrected card came with Nintendo Power. The no-HP copies were not the ones mounted in the magazine, and how they reached collectors isn't known.

The card first came in Japan as a bonus with first pressings of the CD single Meowth's Party in October 1999. Its attack, Miraculous Comeback, flips as many coins as there are Pokémon in play.

_____'s Pikachu, better known as Birthday Pikachu: the blank is for its owner's name, and its attack Birthday Surprise can do 50 more damage on your birthday. Every player who entered Wizards of the Coast's first fan card contest, Create a Baby Pokémon, got one. The contest was a League activity of the second year, open to players who had earned the first badge. Each could design one new Baby Pokémon card; Gym Leaders mailed the entry sheets to Wizards, which sent back the same number of Birthday Pikachus with a thank-you letter. Wizards received far more entries than it expected, and the cards took much longer to arrive than it had estimated.

Kagemaru Himeno drew it. A copy with a Pikachu tail stamp came in the Pikachu World Collection, sold only at Pokémon Park 2000 at the University of Sydney between 12 September and 4 October 2000, alongside the Sydney Olympics.

One of three Pikachu promos the Pokémon League gave out in the summer of 2001, with Pikachu 26 and Surfing Pikachu 28. Its German version came out first, in the Pikachu World Collection, sold only at Pokémon Park 2000 at the University of Sydney between 12 September and 4 October 2000, alongside the Sydney Olympics.

In Japan the same card came with the first issue of Pokémon Card Trainers, the official card magazine, in May 1999, and its Portuguese version came out in the Pikachu World Collection, sold only at Pokémon Park 2000 at the University of Sydney between 12 September and 4 October 2000, alongside the Sydney Olympics.

The new promo of the Colorless season, from August 2002, after the classic Mewtwo 3. Its art won Wizards of the Coast's "Create Your Own Pokémon Card" contest of summer 2001, in which entrants drew an existing Pokémon. It is the only Wizards contest entry ever printed as a card; the winner got the original artwork back with the card in a frame, and extra copies.

Given out in theaters showing Pokémon 4Ever, the fourth film, which opened in the United States on 11 October 2002, the first released by Miramax rather than Warner Bros.; the card carries the film's logo. In Japan, where the film is Celebi: A Timeless Encounter and opened on 7 July 2001, the same card came as promo 006/P, inside the official guidebook to Nintendo Space World 2001 in August 2001.

It has no promo star: it is Mitsuhiro Arita's Jungle Meowth, 56/64, reprinted with a gold border for Pokémon Rolls, a licensed version of Fruit by the Foot sold in the United States from December 1999. Boxes held a card, loose inside: one of four Base Set cards, the three starters and Pikachu, or this Meowth.
